summary: The article profiles Michelle Andrews and Zara McDonald, co-founders of Shameless Media, who met at Mamamia and turned a pop culture podcast idea into a profitable, self-funded company. It covers their friendship, the honest conversations they have as business partners, including about kids and a contingency plan, and the trust they have built with listeners. It also looks at their new advice book, 4am, drawn from the Ask Shameless newsletter, and how it differs from their first book.
one_line: Shameless Media founders Michelle Andrews and Zara McDonald discuss their honest partnership, trust with listeners, and their new advice book 4am.
key_facts: Michelle Andrews and Zara McDonald were both 20 and in entry-level jobs at Mamamia in Melbourne nine years ago, when they bonded over pop culture while sharing Ubers home.
Shameless is described as "a pop culture podcast for smart people who love dumb stuff"; Mamamia rejected the idea at the final hour, which they now say ended up being amazing for them.
Shameless Media launched in 2019 and also hosts the Everybody Has a Secret, Shameless Book Club and Love etc. podcasts.
The company has 1.1 million social media followers, 1 million unique listeners and 2½ million podcast downloads a month.
For the first 10 months Shameless was a weekend project; the pair were self-funded and spent just $70 printing advertising flyers.
Shameless Media has never taken outside investment, was profitable from day one, and has 11 staff.
Andrews married Mitchell Rees last December with McDonald as bridesmaid; McDonald is planning her wedding to Oliver Keogh next year.
To handle the question of having kids, the pair created a contingency plan of growing the team and up-skilling junior employees, so the business does not rely on both showing up at once.
Ask Shameless lands in more than 64,000 subscriber inboxes each Friday, and only five per cent of submitted letters are published.
The new book 4am: Answers to the conundrums that keep you up at night collects the best Ask Shameless columns; their first book, The Space Between, was published in 2020.
Andrews says she wrote the first book believing their words had to mine their darkest events, and wishes she had kept some details of her sexual assault essay to herself.
Andrews says a lot of young women do not receive basic affection, attention or love from male partners, a prevalent issue in the letters.
Andrews says the best advice is often a question that helps someone re-frame; the question she asks herself is "What's the next thing?"
